summary: This bill expands Post-9/11 GI Bill eligibility to National Guard members by amending the definition of qualifying service in 38 U.S.C. 3301 to include full-time National Guard duty and active duty under title 32, with retroactive application to service performed since September 11, 2001.

scores.thoughts: The bill amends 38 U.S.C. § 3301 to expand Post-9/11 GI Bill eligibility to additional categories of National Guard full-time duty (including certain active duty under title 32 and other call-ups). This directly increases the number of service members entitled to federal educational benefits, thereby increasing mandatory federal outlays through the VA. The legislation contains no offsetting cuts or revenue measures. Therefore it expands government spending.
The bill contains no tax provisions, rate changes, credits, or revenue measures of any kind.
The bill addresses only educational assistance benefits; it does not alter health-care programs, coverage, or delivery systems.
No provisions relate to firearms, background checks, or Second Amendment issues.
No immigration, visa, border, or citizenship provisions appear in the text.
The bill is silent on reproductive health services or abortion access.

While the bill concerns National Guard service, it adjusts veterans’ education benefits administered by the VA rather than Department of Defense appropriations or force structure. It does not change defense spending levels.
No environmental, regulatory, or climate-related language is present.

The expanded benefit is a veterans’ education entitlement, not a means-tested welfare program such as SNAP, TANF, or Medicaid. It therefore does not meaningfully affect the conventional social safety net.
The legislation expands a federal veterans’ education benefit but does not address K-12 funding, public schools, school choice, or federal involvement in general education policy.
No drug enforcement, decriminalization, or substance-abuse provisions exist.
The bill contains no sentencing, policing, or criminal-justice reforms.
No trade, tariff, or globalization measures are included.
By increasing mandatory spending without offsets, the bill implicitly accepts additional deficit spending, but the legislation itself does not articulate a debt-reduction or fiscal-policy stance.
No provisions address LGBTQ+ legal protections or related civil-rights issues.
The bill does not mention foreign aid, international assistance, or State Department programs.
No election administration, voting access, or campaign provisions are present.
The legislation contains no technology, data-privacy, or regulatory provisions.
No labor, union, or employment-law changes are included.
The bill does not address religious exemptions, civil-rights enforcement, or anti-discrimination policy.
